source.title: Proving and Improving the Platonic Representation Hypothesis with JEPAs

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Measures cross-model alignment using the Platonic Representation Hypothesis paper’s WIT-1024 protocol, including mutual 10-NN, and tests how it changes with model scale. It also tests alignment under other metrics, training objectives and data conditions.
record.gate_note: Rows capture the reported alignment measurements, scaling comparisons, metric comparisons and demonstrations of mapping independently trained representations. The paper also reports extensive theory and application results. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. Numerous additional encoder sizes, checkpoints, ablations and table entries are omitted under the 60-row cap; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: It reruns the PRH paper's WIT-1024 protocol (mutual 10-NN, max over layers) on language models from 0.5B to 72B against DINOv2, CLIP, MAE and I-JEPA. It adds CKA and a COCO-5k benchmark. It also trains its own text encoders, varying objective, positive views, data and sample count, and tests linear and pair-free maps between separately trained encoders. Most rows are the study's own objective comparisons, which bear on V7 (the training objective and data set the alignment), not on V2's scaling.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also claim to prove a Platonic Representation Theorem: JEPAs whose positives are two observations of one scene learn the same representation up to a rotation. They argue next-token prediction is a bad-view JEPA, which is why language models align with vision only partly and through scale. They conclude that positive views, not scale alone, are the lever. They acknowledge that captioner-generated texts, LeJEPA's departure from the theorem's assumptions, and a SIGReg weight selected on WIT qualify the at-scale comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares independently trained LeJEPA encoders with good or bad positive views against next-token prediction, using mutual 10-NN, CKA, orthogonal mapping and pair-free alignment. It uses the PRH paper’s WIT benchmark protocol but its principal intervention is changing training views and objectives.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment varies with positive-view construction, text source, dataset, training sample count, SIGReg effective weight, whether image positives are frames or crops, and metric/benchmark. The reported scaling law overestimates some long-training good-view runs.

fits_no_version.finding: At 940M-image scale, WIT alignment of the good-view JEPA drops from .184 to .121 when the SIGReg weight is doubled. The weight was then chosen on WIT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Measured cross-modal alignment of a trained encoder is sensitive to its training regularizer hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: The study's empirical scaling law of alignment predicts held-out runs within seed noise (RMSE .0093) but overestimates very long good-view training.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-modal alignment follows a predictable scaling law in samples and fraction of good views.

record.problems: No experiment exactly meets the theorem’s assumptions; the theoretical uniqueness result is for second-order anti-collapse, while experiments use LeJEPA. Many scale comparisons vary data, sample count and batch size together. The largest-scale WIT outcome is sensitive to SIGReg weight, with a weight selected after observing a run. Some Recap texts are image-captioner generated using a vision-language model, and the authors disclose limited benchmark overlap with training data. The empirical scaling law is for one recipe and fails at very long training with good views. Some cited metrics are based on small benchmarks; seed counts vary by comparison.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted additional per-layer and vision-size cells from Tables 15–18, most Flickr retrieval values across web-data scales, detailed MSR-VTT retrieval metrics, nuisance-fraction measurements, numerous ablation settings, captioner decoder/noise variants, and further pair-free classification metrics. These are reported in Sections 3–5 and Tables 2–18; the rows retained prioritize direct alignment outcomes, mixed or absent results, metric/data dependence, and mapping demonstrations.

untested.parts: Shared features or subspaces across seeds of one architecture are not measured.
No interpretable features or circuits are compared.
Model-size scaling is tested only for language models against fixed vision encoders; arbitrary architectures and objectives within one modality are not tested.
Stitching layers and relative representations are not tested.
The number of neighbours k is not varied, and there is no broad out-of-distribution input test beyond Flickr-trained models evaluated on WIT.

missing.what: Language-model scaling on COCO-5k: Qwen2.5 mutual 10-NN .100 (0.5B) to .108 (72B) with DINOv2-B, and CKA .571 to .534. The trend is nearly flat or declining.
Language-model CKA on WIT is non-monotone with size (.318, .324, .363, .353, .333, .336, .418).
Alignment grows with the vision model's size (DINOv2 S/B/L/g, e.g. Qwen2.5-72B .138/.154/.166/.169) and is higher with CLIP image encoders.
Good views at q=1 rise on WIT from .090 to .115 as images go from 0.41M to 50.9M, while bad views stay flat.
missing.locator: Appendix, The scaling law in detail

missing.what: A 200M-image BERT-B good-view JEPA plateaus at .125–.126 from 89M to 160M samples.
An ImageNet ViT-S image JEPA aligns more with DINOv2 (.407 vs .315/.317) and with the text JEPA (.095 vs .079/.080) than the weaker image JEPAs.
missing.locator: Appendix, Image JEPAs trained from scratch; Figure 9 right

missing.what: On WIT, the 33M JEPA's differences from Qwen2.5-3B/7B are within 95% intervals (e.g. +.003 [−.011, +.018]).

record.verdict_notes: The study's main manipulation is the training objective (good vs bad views vs next-token), so most rows bear on V7 rather than V2's scaling. The language-model rows R18–R27 replicate the PRH size trend on WIT, but it is weak and plateaus, and it nearly vanishes on COCO (not recorded). R11, R28 and R29 duplicate each other. The study says good views yield world-state representations, but its own control shows half the at-scale gain comes from captioner-written texts (R39). That supports V7's shared-data explanation. Seed counts vary, and WIT is small enough that the JEPA-versus-LLM comparisons at 50M images are within noise.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments do not establish that independently trained models across arbitrary architectures, objectives, data and modalities converge generally as size and capability increase. Some scale comparisons change data, batch size or other training conditions together.
The study tests image–text alignment in Flickr, MSR-VTT, WIT and COCO settings, but not all vision and language models or a general relation between both models’ capabilities.
It reports seed variation but does not measure shared features or subspaces across independently initialized networks of the same architecture.
Tests orthogonal or orthonormal-row linear maps and a pair-free alignment method in stated settings; does not test stitching layers, relative representations, or all forms of unpaired mapping.
Does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits across models.

Tests mutual 10-NN versus CKA and several datasets and training-data conditions. Does not systematically vary nearest-neighbour count, test broad out-of-distribution inputs, or vary every metric setting.
Tests objective, view and data effects and reports limits to scaling-law extrapolation. Does not isolate every possible contribution of shared training data or objectives across all compared models.
